Ambient music, I am arguing, brings together at a practical level many of the thematic strands I have been discussing, including ambience's connection to rhetoricity. 20 It evokes the concreteness of place through various experiential registers, both for audience and composer, richly enough to constitute what I mean by situation (thought here in terms of Befindlichkeit), the affective, material disposition in which one finds oneself. Thus, the local environs are not background for music's emergence but, in countless ways, an active player in their own right: from the sourcing of found sound (sea bells, insects, or wind and rain); to the acoustic properties of the recording environment, whether "natural" (the previously mentioned Headley Grange for Led Zeppelin) or "artificial" (the drained, empty, electronically produced echo of Joy Division as engineered by the producer Martin Hannett on Unknown Pleasures); to the use of equipment in the composing process itself (turntables for DJs, amplifiers to produce feedback, or tape loops) (see Fuller 13-53); or even to the creation of "impossible'' places realized through the artifice of sound (Eno'sAmbient 4: On Land and Eno and Hass ell's Fourth World, Vol. 1: Possible Musics). The latter point connects back to Clark's assertion about "the ways that the body and the local environment are literally built into the processing loops that result in intelligent action" (Being xii), except here, it is not always action but sometimes experience.

Let me strengthen the connection here between rhetoric, music, and place. The world reveals itself in a musical way, but it does so in such fashion as to transform our experience of place itself. Ambient rhetoric, analogically, brings the world to us but in doing so transforms the disposition of our inhabitancy. This, as I have stated already, is my reworking of what rhetoric is: the world is revealed differently, at least potentially so, in a way that calls for some action. By implication, rhetoric from an ambient perspective can no longer be situated solely in human subjective performance.

Ambient music sounds out the importance of place in conceiving not just rhetoric's performative work but also rhetoricity itself as worldly affectabilityprior to symbolicity.

Indeed, the importance that ambient music attributes to place has wider implications about the power of place as a general and significant matter in its own right. Issues of space and place have gathered momentum in the twentieth century, in the work of Gaston Bachelard, Henri Lefebvre, Alfred North Whitehead, Michel Foucault. Edward Soja, and many more. Heidegger has also been important here, as is borne out especially in the work of Edward Casey, who has done much to put place back into theoretical dis-

cussion (see The Fate of Place). As I discuss in chapter 1, on the chiira, place has since Aristotle largely been conceived categorically and transcendentally, so that place is assimilated to space (Casey x). Heidegger gives back to place its thick particularity; instead of being just another locatable site within a generalized spatial matrix, place becomes habitation. a material. unique location wherein people and things are situated (Casey 20; see also Walter). As Heidegger says, the ambient environs, the '"round-about[.]' is not at all defined by a being-located-side-by-side-and-around-each-other and by geometrical relations, but rather it is the round-about of worldly dealings with it which are concerned about it, attend to it, and go around in it" (0 79). Meaning, affect. and attachment become integral to place, and as ambient music also shows us, "place is indeed an active source ofpresencing: within its close embrace, things get located and begin to happen" (Casey 63). And here we can return full circle to my first, ancient example, the caves at Lascaux. Lascaux is a source of presencing involving the full range of early human existence, including its specific comportment toward aspects of the nonhuman. It is not just a location that happens to be the bearer of early aesthetic and ritualistic designs but a unique place that was integral to their emergence, a kind of window on how the world worlded for them (despite the fact that we may not know the actual details and import of this work). Our traditional sense of aesthetics, among other things, tends to sunder the "art" from the mundane materiality of the cave itself, but this occludes how the material environment is itself already part of what the "art" is. In discussing persuasion, we risk the same reductive move when we exclude the full range of ambient, material phenomena. In short, like everything else, dwelling resists any reduction to forms of simple presence, in this case, to directly available and revealed best practices for homemaking. If we were always already at home, if home were never at issue (never a "thing" for us), then homemaking would not be challenging for us; ultimately it can never be fully realized. Dwelling is an ongoing and never stilled process ofattunement, disclosure, and building. Thus, dwelling is rhetorical in an ambient sense: disclosure and attunement emerge out of a worldly affectability, so that dwelling's coming to manifestation is a matter of ongoing differentiation. In what follows, I will try to elaborate on this point more plainly; specifically, I will try to rethink stability in an ambient key, arguing that it is less a cessation of movement or change than a way of dwelling attuned to sustainability and achieved through the lived realization of sufficiency.

Dwelling in/as Sufficiency

Bringing Heidegger's concept of dwelling into ongoing struggles with sustainability, particularly regarding the automobile, does not just show but performs how humans become cognizant of and organize their practices around what in contemporary environmental discourse we would call an ecology, or things and forces joined together in dynamic coexistence sustainable over time. The English word ecology, which derives from the German Okologie, coined by the biologist Ernst Haeckel in 1866, stems from the ancient Greek word oikos, meaning "house," "home," or "dwelling." Haeckel drew on oikos to bring home the sense of ecology as a comprehensive science of an organism's relation to its environment,

with environment here being where one dwells (Thiele.Indra's 3). As I have shown, when Heidegger discusses dwelling, he describes the relation not only as one of directly co-responding but as one of hearkening to directives or being conditioned by things; for Heidegger, that is, ecology entails more than presence. Ecological literature, however, often describes ecologies in (sometimes overly) holistic terms focused on the powerful role of the feedback loops that emerge within circulating, sustaining activities and material interactions. Feedback loops supply necessary encouragement and constraint allowing for the dynamic self-organization characteristic of a flourishing ecology; this can even be attributed to a direct sense of a "natural" law that we must acknowledge or follow.• Regulatory mechanisms and their "values" are in a sense "built in" to an ecological system. Thus ecologies are often characterized in terms of efficiency, since they tend to reward the maximization of potential. At the same time. ecologies curtail or otherwise redirect efficiency so that nothing gets too far out of balance; if it does, the ecology "self-corrects," adapts, morphs, or fails in accordance with autopoesis, or self-organization (Maturana and Varela, 47-52; Varela, Thompson, and Rosch 88-91: Hayles 136). In short, while efficiency certainly constitutes a vector for an ecology, the notion relevant here can significantly differ from the kind of abstracted and totalized notion of efficiency common to instrumentalized technological thinking,5Efficiency matters because an ecology is at every moment entangled in constraining forces-checks and balances, if you will-necessary for a sustainable trajectory. Insofar as efficiency is thus always tempered, we might better consider it an example of sufficiency. In a sustainable ecological system, efficiency emerges as forms of sufficiency (Thiele, Timely 179).

What is at stake in this qualification of efficiency? We might keep in mind the general definition of efficiency: maximum yield for minimum effort, a point that resonates with Heidegger's arguments about technological enframing insofar as both can be conceived as forms of ordering (QCT 8, 15)_ More precisely, technology already conditions how efficiency is conceived and I ived. This occurs not deterministically but rather ontologically. in shaping how worldly affordances reveal themselves as what they are, for technology is a way of revealing the world, or more pointedly, a revealing that challenges (herausfordern) the world as a standing reserve (Bestand), a stockpile of resources to be exploited (QCT 17). As part of his engagement with technology, the later Heidegger developed a rich notion of dwelling. Dwelling as he uses it entails an ecological attunement to the environment, although it will mean more than this. It differs from, say, the idea that we all have worldviews, which would make dwelling a matter of properly tempering our cultural knowledge. Worldviews, as I have argued, posit a more or less stable common reality variously shaping or shaped by human culture and language. The notion of worldviews invokes the subjective, writ large as society, and thereby gives over to (Western) science the authority to pronounce the truth of nature. A worldview thus constitutes how the world appears "out theren as colored by cultural lenses, a position that insinuates a disengagement between people and world, so that ultimately "objective" reason becomes the means to eliminate cultural distortion and get at the actual essence of things (Ingold 15). 2 As Heidegger argues, however, dwelling indicates not a worldview but a principle of being: culture is materially enworlded. That is, dwelling is a way of being conditioned and permeated by things so that they are inseparable from what it means to live in the world. But dwelling also has a hermeneutic character, in that, like Dasein, questions

of being are continually at issue (see Heidegger, BT 32). The question of how existence is best pursued is not simply given as knowledge but achieved through continual questioning. Such questioning and formulating does not reside solely with the human. Thus, dwelling is not mere survival or existence, nor is it the layering of culture over mundane reality. Dwelling is characterized by thriving or "flourishing" conceived in an ecological key (Heidegger, DT 47). It is not simply an ensemble of practices or habits whose daily performance gets marked by the style we then associate with a particular community. Rather, dwelling indicates lived relations woven into complex ecologies of the world's things and forces. This is not passive coexistence or simple adaptation to things; it is an active if conditioned comportment toward the world. Indeed, this is why Heidegger connects dwelling with building (PLT 146, 148).3By doing so, he grounds human flourishing in constructive activity. That is, the attunement to the world that characterizes dwelling is not passivity. Rather, it is activity that works through and with things as they show up in the world alongside us. Heidegger characterizes this relationship as a dynamic kind of''letting ben appearing as forms of shepherding, cultivating, sparing, and ca retaking (PLT 147-48).

Heidegger's terminology is overly rustic, an important and not unproblematic consideration. Heidegger incorporated such attitudes into much of his thought. When he turned to technological artifacts in his critical ruminations on technology, he often found them to lack a special status he reserved for "things," which were as often as not illustrated through rustic examples. A wine jug is a thing, but a river dam is an object, and in the later Heidegger, the "object" label conveys a negative valuation. I think we must resist this valuation but not simply reject it. Rather, we might ask what stakes lie in making a distinction between a thing and an object. Can this distinction tells us anything that bears on rhetoric and its relation to things and how we dwell with them, even as we move past the limitations we recognize in Heidegger's particular articulation of this distinction? These questions indicate that Heidegger's romanticizations are more than evocations of the rustic. In order to explain this, I want to look at what Heidegger has to say about things and, in particular, how he wants to grant to the thing, as opposed to the object, the ability to manifest what he calls the fourfold (das Geviert). The fourfold is the gathering of earth, sky, mortals, and gods-admittedly a rather oblique statement. In all such partly verbal, partly nonverbal kinds of rhetorical devices, the nonverbal element also persuades by reason of its symbolic character. Paper need not know the meaning of fire in order to burn. But in the "idea" offire there is a persuasive ingredient. By this route something of the rhetorical motive comes to lurk in every "meaning" however purely "scientific" its pretensions. Wherever there is persuasion, there is rhetoric. And wherever there is "meaning," there is "persuasion." Food, eaten and digested, is not rhetorical. But in the meaning o[food there is much rhetoric, the meaning being persuasive enough for the idea of food to be used, like the ideas ofreligion, as a rhetorical device of statesmen. (RM 172-73)

This passage seems far from clear. Additionally, the numerous ironizing quotation marks and italics indicate various forms of pressure and stress. The word meaning, not insignificantly, is italicized twice and twice placed in quotation marks. What does meaning mean here? The most direct reading would be that Burke understands meaning to emerge as our ideas about the world, making meaning the sense or significance of things, events, and relations. Meaning is gleaned from the symbolicity that drapes over (or maybe permeates) the mundane world, circulating it as the significance available to us. The mention of science is important here, for Burke is clearly dissatisfied with a positivist, scientific claim of mere facticity for things of the world, as if measuring qualia sufficed for generating meaning. Thus, he will grant that paper, being paper, has no ideas as such; its rapid oxidation at temperatures around 451 degrees Fahrenheit is a purely chemical reaction. But to remain at this level is to willfully (or methodologically) remain at observation degree zero, and it obscures fire's role in human affairs. When Bradbury's Fireman comes to

burn the books, though, we move into a different realm, one of meaning, and we see that fire is a full rhetorical participant. Fire, then, is more than just a sensed material phenomenon; its integration into the human world necessitates ideas. These ideas mean, and insofar as they mean, they bodily invoke, and insofar as they bodily invoke, they persuade.

As I observed in my discussion of Hawhee, this is not an abstract notion of fire as meaningful; rather, it is one entirely grounded in the bodily integration of ideas stemming from physical experience. As Burke puts it in Attitudes toward History, "our primeval ancestors, by learning language, no longer experienced a sensation solely as a sensation" (382). As he goes on to explain, we may like the warmth ofa fire, and such warmth is certainly a sensation, but as soon as we start putting such experience into language, the words come to "tell a story"; as a result, attitudes (or affective stances) can emerge and be deployed across various forms of discursive interaction, such as the movement from "that feels warm" to the observation that someone is "warm-hearted" (Burke,AH383).

This elevation of meaning over mundane, objective matter is further evinced in other passages. Later in A Rhetoric of Motives Burke again discusses the effect of material phenomena. This time he calls them a form of intuition, and he then tethers intuition to a notion of infancy. One can perceive a seashell, for instance, and note the generative regularity of its spiral. but without more firmly and robustly grasping the intelligibility of that spiral in the world of human meaning, such as reasoning out the mathematical functions that generate various spirals, such an encounter remains stuck in what he terms "infancy," a notion he further compares to the "realm of the unconscious in dreams" (RM 174-75). An "intuition" of spring is not a mere passive perception, a datum of sensory (or even supersensory) knowledge. In terms of an ambient rhetoric, we must not simply turn our sights to sound and ask how we can now use sound to generate desired affective responses. As I stated earlier, we need more than a sonic semiotic. That would certainly be a possibility, but it obscures the deeper insights that sonics thought ambiently can afford us. We can do more with this insight into the ambience of design than single out and focus on various strands, such as the functional (how usable it is), the cognitive (what it means for us), or the affective (how it makes us feel). Instead, we could build a fresh, cumulative list of things with which we might concern ourselves as teachers, writers, and rhetoricians. I have argued that it is better to see them as complexly generating an overarching ambient environment that cradles, without forcing, particular affective responses or that fosters an attunement (as with "clear, confident, and connected," which is Microsoft's take on a positive, secure feeling that will enable work and play). Such a perspective reflects a fuller, less instrumental view of human beings and their interactions, particularly multimedia rhetorics. It deprivileges dir ectly conscious experience and boosts the importance of indirect, unconscious, auratic, osmotic, and ambient phenomena. Put differently, such rhet orical design

organizes an experience, not so much to persuade in any direct sense, but to attune and inflect our sense of bodily inhabitance and the cradle of intelligibility within which we comport ourselves. It is worth recalling Eno's irony-laden dismissal of the corporate sloganeering Microsoft delivered to him as part of the project. If Microsoft perhaps intended more direct forms of marketing and the shaping of the user's experience, including the service of avant-garde musicians to brand Microsoft products, it is important that Eno's music resists such narrowing. For Eno, ambient music is inherently political, evoking new senses of place and how human beings inhabit it; this includes, more pointedly, a reduced role for human agency reflecting a more distributed, ecological approach to will, action, and consequence. The lengthy video session with Robert Fripp and the Microsoft team suggests that such aesthetics and their politics, however indirect, are nevertheless in play. So, while startup music itself makes up only a small element amid these far larger concerns (not to mention the larger expanse of sonic space and its rhetorical-architectural possibilities), possibly one of little relevance, it nevertheless can open us onto a deeper reflection concerning our relation to technology, space, and sonics, and we lose much ifwe ignore the insights it grants.

Rhetoric, Language, Attunement Burke and Heidegger

That which bears itself toward us has already borne our counterbearing into the gift it bears for us.

-Martin Heidegger, "A Dialogue on Language," On the Way to Language

Perhaps the statement "language speaks" is rather obscure but it is certainly no more obscure than the statement "I speak."

-Samuel Ijsseling, Rhetoric and Philosophy in Conflict

There is thus another dimension to persuasion that is as fundamental as the issue Davis hosts for us. Sociality resides. It is always somewhere, and this somewhere can never be fully circumscribed by either meaning or symbolicity. We are worldly. Necessarily, our a priori affectability is not just a transaction among animate beings-humans primarily, but as Davis suggests, also nonhuman animals-so that we see this affectability as enmeshed in material locales that give place and bearing prior to symbolicity proper. All being must be part of the giving of what gives, and the world is what is given, both as meaning and as what withdraws from meaning, even ifworld is not equivalently given. Thus, the challenge of this chapter is to think how rhetoric is caught up in the play of language and materiality while raising the specter that neither language nor materiality can be reduced to symbolicity. Indeed, that is the problem: to what extent can we discuss materiality prior to meaning or symbolicity, and how can we discuss what gives rise to symbolicity as part of symbolicity itself? These questions are themselves problematic from Burke's perspective. Burke almost uniformly places meaning first, and the rhetoricity implicit to symbolic action emerges with it. Heidegger, too, can be and frequently has been read as offering this position, which thus has been taken to mean that world, while certainly material, is always already and only one of significance, making

world inseparable from meaning. I, however, am going to argue that while the world is a world of involvements, and hence meaning, world is also involved in those involvements in ways that are never captured, submerged, or rendered secondary to world as it emerges for human being. This sense of world requires a rich materiality that bears up and stays within human sociality and significance, so that it must also be understood as constituting affective relationality, without, for all that, collapsing into human sociality and significance. Such materiality, as I will show in the upcoming chapters, should always be understood across the play of presence and withdrawal, and human being is only one locus for this play.

When I claim rhetoric is ontological, then, I mean that (1) we come to see that rhetoric cannot be sundered from material being or reduced to epistemological considerations; (2) we understand that rhetoric is intimate with the environments in which it emerges (and not just to which it is joined, as in two separate realms coming together), which grants non humans an elemental role in rhetoricity; (3) this intimacy is not solely a matter of human projection, control. or assignment; and (4) grappling with these entangled, mutually coevolving, and transformative interactions among persons, world, and discourses requires a new appreciation for their constitutive complexity. I can reduce this to a somewhat more succinct statement: rhetoric is a responsive way of revealing the world for others, responding to and put forth through affective, symbolic, and material means, so as to (at least potentially) reattune or otherwise transform how others inhabit the world to an extent that calls for some action (which can include, of course, steadfastness, refusal, or even apathy). Beyond resonating with Davis's approach, my line of thought also bears an affinity to George Kennedy's important essay "A Hoot in the Dark," where Kennedy claims that rhetoric is energy (2). I augment Kennedy, however, by adding that energy is always materialized. Energy emerges within and transforms how one dwells in the world or at least allows for that world to show up, to reveal itself, differently. Ifwe are going to keep to persuasion, then, this is a further intensification of it. Persuasion thought ambiently looks to a materialist affectability that sustains our being-in-the-world. An ambient rhetoric will have taken things at their world and notjust their word.

Many have read Heidegger's remarks on our relations to things as saying that human beings are immersed in the world through language and everyday practices. This perspective suggests, on the one hand, that we cannot break through or extricate ourselves from our emplacement so as to get at things from the "outside," as it were, and, on the other hand, that the things of the world are never trumped by language or ideas. Our holistic entanglements are material and practical first and foremost. Hubert Dreyfus is a well-known proponent of this position and posits Heidegger as a "robust realist," meaning that Heidegger avoids the Scylla ofnaive realism and the Charybdis of idealism ("Coping" n.p.). The world is a participant in the ongoing event of human being-in-the-world, not a stage or backdrop to what human beings do and say. And this is a nuanced participation, with things emerging from and participating in human practices, and human practices in turn requiring things. Such an interpretation is fine as a first take, except that it exhibits a certain skewing: the nexus remains tethered to human being. Human usage and behavior become the privileged means of access to the background, and things, such as tools, light up to our awareness as we use them; then, when our attention shifts elsewhere, they dim back into the shadowy realm of equipment (Zeug) in general, the undifferentiated, always receding backdrop of"stuff."1 Heidegger certainly lends himself to such a reading. Speaking ofa room, he remarks that we encounter it not as a geometrical space but as "equipment for residingp that we have at least discovered, and that discovery and our activities yield

an arrangement that allows individual items to show themselves (BT 98). I take the steps downstairs into the basement, set out my books, organize my papers, boot the laptop, put some Klaus Schulze on the turntable, sit on the chair at the desk, insert the pen drive, enter words into the chapter file (i.e., write), read, take notes, edit, save the file, put on some Dexter Gordon. adjust the stereo volume, and so forth, with aspects of the room now near and now far from my attentions and activities. In various ways, these things all go together; there is an arrangement from which individual entities already derive their place wherefrom I can weave them through my activities. Entities in turn show up and dim back into the recesses as my attention flows variously through my purposeful activity.

In Tool-Being Graham Harman argues that such readings, reminiscent of Dreyfus, are not wrong but nevertheless miss something crucial to the nature of equipment and objects. Objects can no more be positioned solely within the horizon of human intention or awareness than language can. My example of the basement illustrates this tendency, since everything has its "nearness" and "farness" in relation to my attentions and intentions. One could of course add more history here and pile on thick description across the attentions and intentions of other people, social roles, and equipment. But none of this suffices to give us any ultimate grip on the object. Harman argues that "ifwe could total up all the 'contexts, roles, and social goals' in which a specific bridge or flagpole are currently embedded, this would still not give us the being of these objects" (TB 124). Any use or meaning that I or anyone else can bring, or even the plenitude of people, uses, contexts, histories, and other objects that could be brought forward, only serves to present some particular qualities out of the object's fulsomeness, or what Harman calls its "grand, dark abundance" (TB 125). Indeed. as the new wave of cognitive science (such as the work of Andy Clark, Paul Dourish, Anthony Chemero, and so on) demonstrates, the use of tools and local environmental scaffolding inspires changes in our sense of embodiment, blurring boundaries; to use a computer mouse, for instance, amounts to making that mouse part of one's body, and in so doing, it effectively disappears.8 Thus, predicating ontological distinctions on human attention and its shifting cognitive and bodily boundaries is fruitless; the ontological has to manifest beyond such human-derived loci, and thus withdrawal does not depend on human perception or any other singular interaction.

Dwelling, then, entails more than existing and subsisting; it extends beyond simply doing what we need to do-working, socializing, building-to survive to include the richness that is developed and pursued in how we are doing so. Building is not just construction, notjust technics. Nor is it isolable, except at cost, from ambient concerns. To understand place in terms of building necessitates the fullest possible understanding of what makes a location a location. As Heidegger goes on to explain, the fourfold is already wrought with the building of the farmhouse, since the building ofit, which sprang from dwelling, is already a located response to and a living with the fourfold. The farmhouse is built from and sustained by what the earth gives

and lies nestled in the earth's hollows; it receives its direction and temporality from the sky and is further sustained by what the sky brings; the divinities are traced in thankfulness and respect, fear and hope; and death and birth and all the cares of mortals are knit into the house and responsive to the other three aspects of the fourfold, as each of the others similarly join together. None of these things is present in any simple and direct manner. but they can all be seen as gathered in the way of life that gave rise to the farmhouse. Thus, the fourfold cannot be reduced to direct presence, as it is also what remains concealed, although we too often take the mundane persistence of presence as all there is, since it is most near to our everyday concerns. Place is never given in its entirety.

But here we come to the crucial point. This withdrawing is also a form of supporting; it is the repletion of all that is, which in turn ensures that the world is always more than what we make ofit. If the world is to make claims ,on us, ifwe are to dwell in such manner as to attune ourselves to what is noninstrumental. nonrepresentational, then this withdrawal becomes es- :sential. In other words, human knowledge is al ways only partial, and rather tha1\ see this as an invitation to extend knowledge further, as ifwe could pry open all mystery and have it stand revealed before us, Heidegger argues that what remains unconcealed is itself valuable. Dwelling makes being's concealment an occasion for joy and humbleness, thought and insight, guidance and action. It grants the world a kind of meaning or value that, while it cannot speak directly (and hence is neither meaning nor value, exactly), nevertheless calls us in its holding sway and conditions every aspect of our being together. This is the productive "acknowledgment of what is not human in the context of what is" (Thiele, Timely 179). Thus, a location is inseparable from its unique expanse and its ecological connectedness to larger surroundings; all take part in making place a place. Human building arises from place, of course, and is a further disclosure of place, but Heidegger seems to indicate that there is something sound and hale in attuning ourselves to place's role in our constructive pursuits rather than seeking only human-derived, technical, or efficiency-driven projects. I will explore this idea further in the next chapter.

So far I have been arguing that dwelling and the fourfold grant insight into an originary affectability materialized in things and in the world's worlding. Heidegger, of course, would not put it this way (i.e., in t erms of affectability), but we ought not simply transmute affectability into determinism or authoritative demand, as if we could short-circuit dwelling with others in the world into a philosophical version of a command-control
